info.bio: En el invierno entre 1970 y 1971, Bryan Ferry puso un aviso solicitando un teclista para colaborar con el y con Graham Simpson, un bajista que conocía de su banda "The Gas Board". Andy Mackay respondió al aviso, aunque no era teclista sino saxofonista y oboeista, pero tenía un sintetizador VCS3. Andy había conocido a Brian Eno en la universidad (ambos estaban interesados en la música avantgarde y electrónica). Al poco tiempo ambos se encontraron, y como Brian podía tocar el sintetizador, Andy lo convenció para que se uniera a la banda.

scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El costado intelectual del glam. Bowie, «el más grande diletante del rock», fue la inspiración clave del ethos postpunk del cambio constante; Roxy Music y los discos solistas proto-new wave de Brian Eno, con sus ruidos de sintetizador, anticipan el sonido de la década siguiente.
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Rock progresivo
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Al emigrar a Gran Bretaña, el rock se convierte en mercancía de moda pero también se descontextualiza: lo que en EE UU era el diario de la juventud se vuelve en Gran Bretaña un ensayo. El progresivo no comenta la cultura juvenil sino que busca la innovación técnica: arranca con las óperas rock (S.F. Sorrow, Tommy) y los álbumes conceptuales, lo cimentan Traffic, Jeff Beck, Jethro Tull, Family y Genesis, y alcanza su cima con King Crimson (In The Court Of The Crimson King), Van Der Graaf Generator y Yes. Colosseum, la Third Ear Band (inventores de la world music), las variantes góticas (High Tide, Black Widow) y folk (Comus, Strawbs), Gentle Giant, Emerson Lake & Palmer y Roxy Music, que revoluciona el género y prepara la new wave y el synth-pop.

podcast.title: Cream Magazine Review (1973)
podcast.body: A 1973 review in Detroit's Cream Magazine criticized Roxy Music's debut album, describing its artifice as potentially "unhealthy as the sheen on a piece of rotten meat" and noting Side Two's excessive reliance on Brian Eno's synthesizer, which "leans a little too heavily on the synthesizer... without the saving grace of drums and bass line." Despite the harsh critique, this divisiveness made them appealing to a niche audience. "From the drag queen on the corner, to the fop finery in the centerfold, to the polished deformity of the music on the record, this celebrates the kind of artifice that could come to seem as unhealthy as the sheen on a piece of rotten meat."

podcast.title: Early Live Performance Critique (1973)
podcast.body: Music critic Tony Palmer, reviewing a Roxy Music live show in the spring of 1973 after the release of two albums, called their albums "overproduced." However, he described the live performance as "demonic sinister apocalyptic, monstrous, dazzling flashy. What opera might have been in the 1970s had it not lost its nerve." Palmer's review also included a warning against the band resorting to gimmicks or selling out. "The group was, and I quote, demonic sinister apocalyptic, monstrous, dazzling flashy."

podcast.title: Contemporary Critical Reception
podcast.body: In the 1970s, critical reception for Roxy Music was sharply divided, described as a "love it or hate it" situation. John Wadsworth, writing for *The Daily Tar Heel* in 1974, offered glowing praise, calling Roxy Music "the mating of the electronic with the lucid rock in the dimensionless bed of the avant-garde" and comparing Brian Ferry's voice to "divine impulses that have blessed our senses with William Blake and Sun Ra." "no earthly voice compares to Brian Ferry's."

podcast.body: Roxy Music is recognized as a bridge between glam rock and punk, a genre that gained significant popularity by the end of the 1970s. Their music was often described by critics as more sophisticated than that of bands like T. Rex or Sweet, and it also resonated with 80s new wave fans. "Roxy Music was kind of a bridge between glam and punk, which was very popular, of course, at the end of the 70s."

podcast.body: Roxy Music is credited with taking glam rock a step further and, in many ways, reinventing rock music, challenging the notion that glam was merely about theatrics. An article in *The Economist* posited that the only reason the band isn't praised as much as David Bowie for their historical contributions is that their debut album was released on the same day as Bowie's *Ziggy Stardust*. "Roxy Music took it a step further, and in many ways reinvented rock."

xref.title: Transition to Ambient Music
xref.body: Brian Eno, originally from a rock background with Roxy Music, embarked on solo experiments in ambient music, which diverged significantly from rock. His work emphasized atmospherics, textures, repetition, and sought to create a "mode" rather than tell stories with lyrics, often without lyrics at all.
